content.prompt:
In a triathlon race, Luca ran at an average speed 5 times his average swimming speed. Also, when his average running speed was multiplied by 4, this number was 3 less than his average speed for the cycling leg.

If $x$ km/h is Luca’s average swimming speed, find expressions in terms of $x$ for his:

answer.worked:
Luca’s average running speed is 5 times his average swimming speed.

$$\text{Running speed}=5x\text{ km/h}$$

Four times the running speed is 3 km/h less than the cycling speed, so add 3 km/h.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Cycling speed}&=4(5x)+3\\\text{Cycling speed}&=(20x+3)\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: Both parts translate verbal relationships into expressions without solving an equation. Part b substitutes the running-speed expression from part a into the cycling-speed relationship.

inlines.text: Match each of the following mathematical expressions with its corresponding English expression.
i   Six less than four times
ii   Three times one more than
iii   Two less than one-quarter of
iv   One-quarter of two less than
v   Four less than twice
vi   Six more than half of
vii   One more than three times
viii   Five less than
ix   Six more than
x   Four more than twice

answer.worked: Twice $x$ is $2x$; four more is $4+2x$. Match: x.
Five less than $x$ is $x-5$. Match: viii.
Twice $x$ is $2x$; four less is $2x-4$. Match: v.
One more than $x$ is $x+1$; three times this is $3(x+1)$. Match: ii.
Four times $x$ is $4x$; six less is $4x-6$. Match: i.
One-quarter of $x$ is $\frac{x}{4}$; two less is $\frac{x}{4}-2$. Match: iii.
Two less than $x$ is $x-2$; one-quarter of this is $\frac{x-2}{4}$. Match: iv.
Six more than $x$ is $x+6$. Match: ix.
Three times $x$ is $3x$; one more is $3x+1$. Match: vii.
Half of $x$ is $\frac{x}{2}$; six more is $\frac{x}{2}+6$. Match: vi.

content.prompt: Solve these equations for $x$ and check your answers.

answer.worked:
Multiply both sides by 4.

$$\begin{align*}3x-4&=2x+12\\x-4&=12\\x&=16\end{align*}$$

Check:

$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{3(16)}{4}-1\\&=11\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{16}{2}+3\\&=11\end{align*}$$

Both sides are equal.

Multiply both sides by 3.

$$\begin{align*}x+6&=4x+9\\-3&=3x\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$

Check:

$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{-1}{3}+2\\&=\frac{5}{3}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{4(-1)}{3}+3\\&=\frac{5}{3}\end{align*}$$

Both sides are equal.

Multiply both sides by 6.

$$\begin{align*}5x-18&=42-2x\\7x-18&=42\\7x&=60\\x&=\frac{60}{7}\end{align*}$$

Check:

$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{5}{6}\left(\frac{60}{7}\right)-3\\&=\frac{29}{7}\\\text{RHS}&=7-\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{60}{7}\right)\\&=\frac{29}{7}\end{align*}$$

Both sides are equal.

Multiply both sides by 15.

$$\begin{align*}5x-60&=90-6x\\11x-60&=90\\11x&=150\\x&=\frac{150}{11}\end{align*}$$

Check:

$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{150}{11}\right)-4\\&=\frac{6}{11}\\\text{RHS}&=6-\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{150}{11}\right)\\&=\frac{6}{11}\end{align*}$$

Both sides are equal.

Multiply both sides by 12.

$$\begin{align*}20-6x&=9x+14\\6&=15x\\x&=\frac{2}{5}\end{align*}$$

Check:

$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\\&=\frac{22}{15}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)+\frac{7}{6}\\&=\frac{22}{15}\end{align*}$$

Both sides are equal.

Multiply both sides by 12.

$$\begin{align*}11-10x&=9x-8\\19&=19x\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

Check:

$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{11}{12}-\frac{5(1)}{6}\\&=\frac{1}{12}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{3(1)}{4}-\frac{2}{3}\\&=\frac{1}{12}\end{align*}$$

Both sides are equal.

content.prompt: During a power failure, Sonia lights two identical candles of length 10 cm at 7 p.m. One candle burns out by 11 p.m. and the other candle burns out at 12 midnight. Assume that the length of each candle goes down by a constant rate.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How high is each candle at 8 p.m.?

answer.short: 11 p.m. candle: $7.5\text{ cm}$; midnight candle: $8\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
The candles burn for 4 hours and 5 hours respectively, so their rates of decrease are $10\div4=2.5\text{ cm/h}$ and $10\div5=2\text{ cm/h}$. At 8 p.m., 1 hour has elapsed.

11 p.m. candle: $10-2.5\times1=7.5\text{ cm}$.

Midnight candle: $10-2\times1=8\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How high is each candle at 9 p.m.?

answer.short: 11 p.m. candle: $5\text{ cm}$; midnight candle: $6\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
At 9 p.m., 2 hours have elapsed.

11 p.m. candle: $10-2.5\times2=5\text{ cm}$.

Midnight candle: $10-2\times2=6\text{ cm}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How high is each candle $t$ hours after 7 p.m.?

answer.short: 11 p.m. candle: $(10-2.5t)\text{ cm}$ for $0\le t\le4$; midnight candle: $(10-2t)\text{ cm}$ for $0\le t\le5$. Each candle has height 0 after it burns out.
answer.worked:
Height remaining = initial height − rate of decrease × time.

11 p.m. candle: $(10-2.5t)\text{ cm}$ for $0\le t\le4$.

Midnight candle: $(10-2t)\text{ cm}$ for $0\le t\le5$.

Each candle has height 0 after it burns out.

children.label: d
children.prompt: At what time is one candle twice as high as the other candle?

answer.short:
10:20 p.m.

Set the slower-burning candle's height equal to twice the faster-burning candle's height.
answer.worked:
Let $t$ be the number of hours after 7 p.m. The midnight candle is taller because it burns more slowly.

$$\begin{align*}10-2t&=2(10-2.5t)\\10-2t&=20-5t\\10+3t&=20\\3t&=10\\t&=\frac{10}{3}\end{align*}$$

$\frac{10}{3}$ hours is 3 hours 20 minutes, so the time is 10:20 p.m. The heights are $\frac{10}{3}\text{ cm}$ and $\frac{5}{3}\text{ cm}$, confirming the required ratio.

content.prompt: Ten $\text{cm}^3$ of silver and $5\text{ cm}^3$ of copper weigh $150\text{ g}$. One cubic centimetre of silver weighs $1\frac{1}{6}$ times as much as $1\text{ cm}^3$ of copper. Find the weight of $1\text{ cm}^3$ of each of the metals.

inlines.text: Silver:
; copper:
per cubic centimetre.
Express the silver’s unit mass in terms of the copper’s, then equate the combined mass to 150 g.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ grams be the weight of $1\text{ cm}^3$ of copper. Then $1\text{ cm}^3$ of silver weighs $\frac{7x}{6}$ grams.

The combined weight is $150\text{ g}$, so
$$\begin{align*}10\left(\frac{7x}{6}\right)+5x&=150\\70x+30x&=900\\100x&=900\\x&=9.\end{align*}$$
Thus $1\text{ cm}^3$ of copper weighs $9\text{ g}$.

For silver,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{7x}{6}&=\frac{7\times9}{6}\\&=10.5.\end{align*}$$
Thus $1\text{ cm}^3$ of silver weighs $10.5\text{ g}$.

content.prompt: A river flows at 5 km/h. A boat goes upstream half as fast as downstream. What is the speed of the boat in still water?

answer.short:
$15\text{ km/h}$.

Subtract the current speed upstream and add it downstream; the upstream speed is half the downstream speed.
answer.worked:
Let $v$ be the boat’s speed in still water, in km/h. Its upstream speed is $(v-5)$ km/h and its downstream speed is $(v+5)$ km/h.

$$\begin{align*}v-5&=\frac{v+5}{2}\\2v-10&=v+5\\v-10&=5\\v&=15\end{align*}$$

The boat’s speed in still water is $15\text{ km/h}$. Upstream it travels at $10\text{ km/h}$ and downstream at $20\text{ km/h}$, so the upstream speed is half the downstream speed.

content.prompt: Twenty litres of milk with unknown butter-fat content from vat A is mixed with 10 litres of milk with $3\%$ butter-fat from vat B to produce milk with $3\frac{3}{4}\%$ butter-fat content. Find the percentage of butter-fat in vat A.

answer.short:
$4\frac{1}{8}\%$.

Equate the total butter-fat before and after mixing.
answer.worked:
Let $x\%$ be the butter-fat content of the milk in vat A. The mixture contains $30$ litres. Conserving the volume of butter-fat gives
$$\begin{align*}
20\left(\frac{x}{100}\right)+10\left(\frac{3}{100}\right)&=30\left(\frac{15}{400}\right)\\
\frac{x}{5}+\frac{3}{10}&=\frac{9}{8}\\
8x+12&=45\\
8x&=33\\
x&=\frac{33}{8}\\
x&=4\frac{1}{8}.
\end{align*}$$
The butter-fat content in vat A is $4\frac{1}{8}\%$.

content.prompt: The ends of a bar have to be machined down until the bar is $3$ m long. After $5\%$ of the length had been removed, it was found that $0.5\%$ of the new length still had to come off. What length was removed at each machining and what was the original length of the bar?

inlines.text: First machining:
; second machining:
; original length:
The remaining length is 95% of the original after the first machining, then 99.5% of that length after the second.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ m be the original length. After the first machining, the length is $\frac{19x}{20}$ m. After the second machining, $\frac{199}{200}$ of that length remains.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{199}{200}\times\frac{19x}{20}&=3\\\frac{3781x}{4000}&=3\\3781x&=12000\\x&=\frac{12000}{3781}=3\frac{657}{3781}.\end{align*}$$

The first machining removes
$$\begin{align*}\frac{5}{100}\times\frac{12000}{3781}&=\frac{600}{3781}\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

The length after the first machining is
$$\begin{align*}\frac{19}{20}\times\frac{12000}{3781}&=\frac{600}{199}\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

The second machining removes
$$\begin{align*}\frac{0.5}{100}\times\frac{600}{199}&=\frac{3}{199}\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

Thus the machining lengths are $\frac{600}{3781}$ m and $\frac{3}{199}$ m, respectively, and the original length is $3\frac{657}{3781}$ m.

content.prompt: A salesman makes a trip to visit a client. The traffic he encounters keeps his average speed to 40 km/h. On the return trip, he takes a route 6 km longer, but he averages 50 km/h. If he takes the same time each way, how long was the total journey?

answer.short:
54 km.

Use distance = average speed × time and the equal journey times.
answer.worked:
Let $t$ hours be the time taken each way. The outward distance is $40t$ km and the return distance is $50t$ km. The return route is 6 km longer.

$$\begin{align*}50t&=40t+6\\10t&=6\\t&=0.6\end{align*}$$

The outward distance is $40\times0.6=24$ km and the return distance is $50\times0.6=30$ km.

Total distance $=24+30=54$ km.

entries.description:
We have seen that many real-world problems can be converted to equations. We have also seen how to solve simple equations. In this chapter, we consider a wider variety of equations and use them to solve practical problems.

Equations arise naturally when solving problems. In fact, a lot of problem-solving relies on us being able to translate a given word or real world problem into an equation, or equations, solve the equation(s) and relate the solution to the original problem. Turning a complicated problem into an equation enables us to understand and solve difficult problems. Before we reach this stage, we need to have at hand a collection of techniques for solving equations.

In earlier times, people used a number of ad hoc methods for solving equations. Only since the development of modern algebra have standard procedures and notations been introduced that enable us to solve equations quickly and efficiently.

entries.description:
Let t hours be the time for the cycle leg.
Then 2t hours is the time for the running leg and (4 1/4 − t − 2t) hours is the time for the swim leg.
Now, distance of run + distance of cycle + distance of swim = total distance,
so 10 × 2t + 40 × t + 2 1/2 × (4 1/4 − t − 2t) = 50
20t + 40t + (5/2)(17/4 − 3t) = 50
60t + 85/8 − 15t/2 = 50
480t + 85 − 60t = 400
420t = 315
t = 315/420
t = 3/4
The athlete takes 3/4 hour, or 45 minutes, to complete the cycle leg.

entries.description:
The symbol ≤ means ‘is less than or equal to’.
The symbol ≥ means ‘is greater than or equal to’.
The statement ‘4 ≤ 6’ means that either ‘4 < 6’ or ‘4 = 6’ is true. It is correct because the statement ‘4 < 6’ is true. It does not matter that the second statement, ‘4 = 6’, is false.
It is also correct to say that 3 ≥ 3, because the statement ‘3 = 3’ is true. Once again, it does not matter that the statement ‘3 > 3’ is false.
Statements such as ‘−6 < 2’, ‘5 > 3’, ‘4 ≤ 6’ and ‘3 ≥ 3’ are called inequalities.

entries.description:
Solving the linear inequality 4x − 5 < 3 means finding all of the values for x that satisfy that inequality.
It is easy to find some numbers that satisfy the inequality. For example, if x = −2,
4x − 5 = −13 < 3
Similarly, if x = 0,
4x − 5 = −5 < 3
However, x = 4 does not satisfy the inequality, because when x = 4,
4x − 5 = 11 > 3
So x = −2 and x = 0 satisfy the inequality, but x = 4 does not.
There is a systematic way of solving linear inequalities, as shown in the following examples. We often graph the solution set on the number line.
The method for solving linear inequalities is the same as that for solving linear equations, except for multiplying and dividing both sides by a negative number.
